clue.text: Leave about ten, love, with one cent? How impracticably romantic!

indicators.note: about means going round, so the word for leave is wrapped around what follows

parts.note: to quit is to leave
X is the Roman numeral for ten
love is nil in tennis, shaped like the letter O
I is the Roman numeral for one
C is the standard abbreviation for cent

explanation.surface: Someone quits leaving a pitiful tip of a few coins and a cent, and the onlooker sighs at such dreamy folly.
explanation.walkthrough: QUIT goes round X and O to make QUIXOT, then I and C are added on the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Named after Don Quixote, the adjective describes idealistic schemes pursued without regard to practicality.

clue.text: Rude if remarkably Scottish variety of hut

indicators.note: a variety is a different form of something, so these letters come in a different arrangement

parts.note: unco is the Scots word for remarkably or very
the three letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A Highland shelter is described as remarkably crude.
explanation.walkthrough: Unco is a Scots adverb meaning very or uncommonly, as in 'unco guid'; it leads, followed by the shuffled hut.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacking manners or refinement, coarse in behaviour, is the plain sense of the adjective.

clue.text: Whence air from the wood, though not wood wind

definitions.text: Whence air from the wood, though not wood wind

parts.words: Whence air from the wood, though not wood wind
parts.note: surface reading: a breeze blowing out of a forest, or a woodwind instrument such as a clarinet
setter's reading: a tune struck from wooden bars, an instrument whose Greek name means wood-sound

explanation.walkthrough: Air is a tune, and the instrument is played by striking wooden bars, so it makes music from wood without any wind at all.
explanation.definitionFit: A percussion instrument of tuned wooden bars struck with mallets; the Greek roots mean wood and sound.

clue.text: Two birds, excluding the tern, make a tasty morsel

parts.note: the first bird, a small songbird

indicators.note: excluding means leaving out, so the named seabird's letters are removed from the second bird

parts.note: the second bird, a marsh-dwelling heron
the seabird to be taken out

explanation.surface: Two birds, minus one seabird, make a fine dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Two birds' supplies both birds at once; the tern named afterwards is struck out of the longer, marsh-dwelling one.
explanation.definitionFit: A small choice piece of food, or by extension a juicy item of gossip, is the British word here.

clue.text: Variation in one's speech when one moves house?

definitions.text: Variation in one's speech when one moves house?

parts.note: setter's reading: an address is also a formal speech, so altering it is a variation in what one says
surface reading: the paperwork a household faces on moving to a new home

explanation.walkthrough: Address means both where you live and a formal speech, so the phrase works for moving home and for altering a talk.
explanation.definitionFit: The notice sent out on moving home tells friends and offices the new place where letters should reach you.

clue.text: The Blackstone boy, a drop-out?

parts.note: jet is a black stone, a hard black lignite used in jewellery
a boy's name

explanation.surface: A youngster from the Blackstone family has left school or society.
explanation.walkthrough: Blackstone looks like a surname (Sir William Blackstone, the legal writer), but it splits into black stone.
explanation.definitionFit: Goods thrown overboard from a ship to lighten it are those dropped out of the vessel into the sea.

clue.text: Symbol of Prussian might — hard to remove without its transposition

indicators.note: transposition means swapping places, so the front and back halves of the device's name change round

parts.note: a bootjack is the forked device used to pull off tight riding boots, which are hard to remove without one

explanation.surface: The emblem of Prussian militarism cannot be shed without some trick.
explanation.walkthrough: BOOTJACK with its halves swapped becomes JACKBOOT, the very boot a bootjack helps you take off.
explanation.definitionFit: The tall military boot of Prussian and later German soldiers became a byword for authoritarian bullying force.

clue.text: Old magistrate after learning to be a pavement artist

indicators.note: after says the magistrate comes behind, placed second in the line

parts.note: Sc is the abbreviation for science, whose root sense is knowledge or learning
a reeve was a medieval English local magistrate or official

explanation.surface: A retired judge takes up chalk drawing on the footpath after some study.
explanation.walkthrough: Sc for science, as in BSc, stands in for learning; the reeve is the old official of an English shire or manor.
explanation.definitionFit: A screever draws chalk pictures on pavements for coins, and the verb names that street activity.

clue.text: This night perchance to dream up a clue for 2000

definitions.text: This night perchance to dream up a clue for 2000

parts.note: surface reading: Hamlet's 'perchance to dream', pointing to Shakespeare's play about a night of dreaming in the woods near Athens
setter's reading: the centre of the warm season's name holds MM, the Roman numerals for two thousand

explanation.walkthrough: The answer completes the title of Shakespeare's play about a night's dream, and its middle letters read literally give MM, Roman 2000.
explanation.definitionFit: The play's title names the night around the summer solstice, a season of fairies and enchantment in folklore.

clue.text: Fur returned to the French firm

indicators.note: returned means sent back, so the whole string of letters is read from right to left

parts.note: taken as written
le is French for the
Co is the abbreviation for company

explanation.surface: A fur coat is sent back to a firm in France.
explanation.walkthrough: TO LE CO read backwards gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The ocelot is a spotted wild cat of the Americas whose pelt was prized for coats, so it names the fur.

clue.text: Held, by a fluke, a job in the house and outside

indicators.note: outside says the conjunction sits round the household job, enclosing it

parts.note: taken as written
a chore is a routine household task

explanation.surface: Someone landed a domestic post by sheer luck.
explanation.walkthrough: By a fluke looks like by chance, but a fluke is also the barbed blade of an anchor that grips the seabed.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship held fast by the fluke of its anchor biting into the seabed is moored securely in place.

clue.text: How foreigners flood the home market with fish or suet?

parts.words: How foreigners flood the home market
parts.note: foreign producers dump cheap goods on a market, selling below cost
the ling is a long sea fish of the cod family

explanation.surface: A question about how overseas sellers swamp local trade with cheap fish or cooking fat.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the definition by example: suet is the main ingredient of the British boiled ball of dough.
explanation.definitionFit: A suet pudding ball, flour and suet boiled in a stew, is the classic British example, so suet hints at it.

clue.text: Foreign Office furniture

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a government department or agency, a word borrowed from French
second meaning: a writing desk with drawers

explanation.walkthrough: Foreign Office is the British ministry, but here foreign signals a borrowed word for an office.
explanation.definitionFit: The French loanword covers both an administrative department and a desk with a sloping lid and drawers.

clue.text: War-cry of TV doctor at work

parts.note: Doctor Who, the long-running BBC science-fiction hero
op is short for opus, a musical work

explanation.surface: A television doctor bellows a battle-cry while on the job.
explanation.definitionFit: A loud shout of excitement or a warrior's yell, as in the whooping of a charge into battle.

clue.text: George R. Sims's Christ mas scene

definitions.text: George R. Sims's Christ mas scene

parts.words: George R. Sims's Christ mas scene
parts.note: surface reading: the setting of some festive tableau by a Victorian writer
setter's reading: Christmas Day', set among the destitute

explanation.walkthrough: George R. Sims's 1877 poem opening 'It is Christmas Day in the Workhouse' was endlessly recited and parodied; the space in Christ mas is a printing slip.
explanation.definitionFit: The Victorian institution where paupers were housed and set to labour is the place where the ballad unfolds.

clue.text: Converted soul comes to face lions here?

definitions.text: Converted soul comes to face lions here?
definitions.note: the whole clue describes the arena where Christians met the lions

indicators.note: converted means changed into another form, so the letters following are recast

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A Christian convert arrives at the place where martyrs were thrown to the lions.
explanation.walkthrough: Converted does double duty: it rearranges the letters and describes the Christian convert who faced the beasts.
explanation.definitionFit: Rome's great amphitheatre is traditionally where early Christians were executed by wild animals before crowds.

clue.text: Where Johnny hoped to see stars?

definitions.text: Where Johnny hoped to see stars?

parts.words: Where Johnny hoped to see stars?
parts.note: surface reading: a boy hoping to gaze at the night sky
setter's reading: a Johnny in old slang was a young man-about-town who waited outside theatres to court actresses

explanation.walkthrough: A Johnny of this kind hung about the theatre's back entrance for a glimpse of the leading ladies.
explanation.definitionFit: The rear entrance of a theatre used by performers is where admirers wait to meet the stars of a show.

clue.text: John Frenchman is liable to croak

definitions.note: describes the creature rather than naming it

parts.note: John Bull is the personification of England
frog is an old disparaging nickname for a Frenchman

explanation.surface: An Englishman and a Frenchman together look likely to die.
explanation.walkthrough: Croak suggests dying, but here it is the deep call of a large amphibian.
explanation.definitionFit: This large North American amphibian is famous for its loud booming call, so croaking is its habit.

clue.text: About to take S American country girl to the second reading

parts.note: re means about or concerning
Peru is in South America
a girl's name, short for Sally

explanation.surface: Someone is about to take a South American girl to a play-reading.
explanation.walkthrough: About looks like 'on the point of', but it is the short word meaning concerning.
explanation.definitionFit: Perusal is a careful reading, so going through a text again is a fresh perusal of it.

clue.text: Milady's hippie basket

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a framework worn under a lady's skirt to spread it out at the hips
second meaning: one of a pair of baskets slung over a pack animal or bicycle

explanation.walkthrough: Hippie looks like the 1960s flower child, but here it means something for the hips; the hoop under an eighteenth-century skirt bulged out at the sides.
explanation.definitionFit: The word covers both a hip-widening hooped skirt frame and a carrier basket hung beside a saddle or wheel.

clue.text: An elevator say, in the bathroom?

definitions.note: points to an item found in a bathroom rather than naming it

indicators.note: say asks us to speak the word, using its sound rather than its spelling

parts.note: an elevator is something that lifts, a raiser

explanation.surface: A question about whether there is a lift in the bathroom.
explanation.walkthrough: Elevator looks like a lift, but it is simply something that raises.
explanation.definitionFit: A bladed shaving tool is a standard bathroom item, kept by the basin for the morning shave.

clue.text: Monkey-talk by the man with the hypodermic

definitions.meaning: second meaning: one who jabs, giving injections

explanation.walkthrough: The second meaning is a whimsical coinage: someone who jabs with a needle.
explanation.definitionFit: Rapid meaningless chatter like a monkey's gibbering, and literally a person who gives jabs with a needle.

clue.text: George Frederick barred water

parts.note: surface reading: a man named George Frederick forbade swimming or blocked a stream
setter's reading: he set water in musical bars, writing the Water Music for King George I

explanation.walkthrough: George Frideric is the composer's forename pair, and his Water Music was played on the Thames; barred means written out in bars.
explanation.definitionFit: The German-born British baroque composer of Messiah and the Water Music bore the forenames George Frideric.

clue.text: The longest chord in non musical circles

definitions.text: The longest chord in non musical circles

parts.words: The longest chord in non musical circles
parts.note: surface reading: a sustained harmony among people who are not musicians
setter's reading: in geometry a chord is a line joining two points on a circle

explanation.walkthrough: Chord and circles both suggest music, but the clue says non-musical: geometry's straight line across a circle.
explanation.definitionFit: The straight line through a circle's centre joining two points on its edge is the longest possible chord.

clue.text: Eve's ruin involved all creation

indicators.note: involved means tangled up, so these letters are twisted into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Eve's fall in Eden brought down the whole of creation with her.
explanation.definitionFit: Everything that exists, the cosmos and all its matter and space, is what all of creation amounts to.

clue.text: Phone Boreas for ex ample

definitions.meaning: first meaning: British slang for the telephone
second meaning: something that blows; Boreas is the Greek god of the north wind

explanation.walkthrough: Phone looks like a verb telling you to ring Boreas; the space in ex ample is a printing slip.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for a telephone, and literally one that blows, as the wind god puffs out the north wind.

clue.text: Operator of pincer movements near Wigan apparently

indicators.note: apparently means visible on the surface, so the letters lie in plain sight in the words before it

parts.note: the run of letters straddling the two words

explanation.surface: A military commander runs encircling manoeuvres close to Wigan, a town in Lancashire.
explanation.walkthrough: Pincer movements sound military, but here they are the snapping of an insect's tail forceps.
explanation.definitionFit: This insect carries a pair of forceps-like pincers on its tail, so it literally works pincers.

clue.text: Two lovely black eves!

parts.note: surface reading: admiring a pair of dark evenings, a misprint for eyes
setter's reading: the music-hall song 'Two lovely black eyes', whose next line is 'Oh, what a ...!'

explanation.walkthrough: The 1886 music-hall song goes 'Two lovely black eyes, Oh, what a surprise!'; eves is a printing slip for eyes.
explanation.definitionFit: The song's chorus answers the black eyes with an exclamation of shock at something unexpected happening.
